flashcards.q: Name the first four integer argument registers in System V x86-64 and AAPCS64.
flashcards.a: System V x86-64: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx (then r8, r9 for args 5-6). AAPCS64: x0, x1, x2, x3 (through x7 for args 5-8).

flashcards.q: Where do floating-point arguments go relative to integer arguments on x86-64/ARM64?
flashcards.a: A separate register file, numbered independently: xmm0-xmm7 on x86-64, v0-v7 on ARM64. A mixed int/float function's registers are not interleaved into one combined sequence.

flashcards.q: Distinguish caller-saved from callee-saved registers on x86-64 System V.
flashcards.a: Caller-saved (rax,rcx,rdx,rsi,rdi,r8-r11): callee may freely clobber, caller must save what it needs across the call. Callee-saved (rbx,rbp,r12-r15): callee must restore to original value before returning.

flashcards.q: Why can an ARM64 leaf function skip stack frame setup entirely, unlike x86-64?
flashcards.a: ARM64's bl instruction stores the return address in a dedicated register (x30/lr), so a leaf function can work entirely in registers and ret directly. x86-64's call always pushes the return address to the stack, so even the leanest function needs ret to pop it back off.

flashcards.q: What does -fomit-frame-pointer (default at -O2+) do, and what production capability does it break?
flashcards.a: Repurposes rbp as a general register instead of a frame pointer, saving one register but breaking naive rbp-chain-walking backtraces/profilers -- fixed with -fno-omit-frame-pointer or DWARF CFI (.eh_frame)-based unwinding.

flashcards.q: A function crashes only at -O2, not -O0. First hypothesis and how to confirm?
flashcards.a: Undefined behavior (signed overflow, uninitialized read, strict-aliasing violation) that -O0's minimal transformation happened to hide but -O2's aggressive optimization exposes. Confirm with -fsanitize=undefined,address, not by blaming the compiler.

flashcards.q: List the four stacked costs that make a naive CPython arithmetic loop ~50-100x slower than C.
flashcards.a: Bytecode dispatch overhead, boxed PyObject allocation per result, reference counting on every object touch, and dynamic __add__ method dispatch -- none of which exist in a compiled C loop.

flashcards.q: Is 'Python is 100x slower than C' true for all Python code?
flashcards.a: No -- it's true for the interpreter loop's per-element overhead in pure-Python numeric loops. Code whose hot path runs inside a C extension (NumPy, most stdlib internals) pays essentially none of that per-element cost.

flashcards.q: How does the Windows x64 calling convention differ materially from System V x86-64?
flashcards.a: Only 4 register arguments (rcx,rdx,r8,r9 vs System V's 6), a caller-allocated 32-byte shadow space even when args fit in registers, and a different caller/callee-saved split -- making Windows and Linux/macOS x86-64 object code ABI-incompatible on identical hardware.

flashcards.q: What does it look like in objdump when a function call was fully inlined and optimized away?
flashcards.a: No call instruction to the target's label -- its logic appears directly inline in the caller's instruction stream, and if inputs are compile-time-constant, the whole computation can collapse to a single mov of a precomputed value.

flashcards.q: Why might a summing loop compile at -O2 to code with no loop at all?
flashcards.a: The optimizer recognizes a closed-form arithmetic series (e.g. n*(n-1)/2) via strength reduction and induction-variable analysis and replaces the loop with a direct formula computation -- only possible when the loop body is provably side-effect-free.

flashcards.q: What's the cost-benefit case for enabling -fno-omit-frame-pointer fleet-wide?
flashcards.a: Cost: small, typically low-single-digit percent throughput regression from dedicating rbp to frame bookkeeping. Benefit: reliable perf-based production profiling/stack unwinding across the fleet -- worth it when continuous production profiling is a core operational capability.
